explain.say: Instead of a clutch pedal, many automatics use a torque converter: a pump spun by the engine flings oil at a turbine joined to the gearbox. The oil link can slip, so the car can sit still in gear with the engine running.

faq.q: How does an automatic gearbox know when to change gear?
faq.a: Sensors measure road speed, accelerator position and engine speed. A computer compares them with its programs and shifts up as you speed up, or down when you press hard to overtake.
asks: How does an automatic decide the gear?

faq.q: What is the transmission control unit?
faq.a: It is a small computer that decides when to change gear. It works the valves that direct oil pressure inside the gearbox.
asks: Is there a computer in the gearbox?

faq.q: Why does an automatic gearbox use oil?
faq.a: Oil does three jobs: under pressure it squeezes the clutches that select gears, it carries power through the torque converter, and it lubricates and cools the gears.
asks: What is automatic transmission fluid for?

faq.q: What is a planetary gear set?
faq.a: A planetary gear set has a central sun gear, small planet gears around it and an outer ring gear. Holding one part still and driving another gives different speeds, so a few sets give many gears.
A torque converter replaces the clutch pedal. An engine-driven pump flings oil onto a turbine linked to the gearbox, so power flows through the oil and the car can stop in gear without stalling.
asks: Why doesn't an automatic car stall?

facts: A planetary gear set gives different ratios depending on which of its parts, sun, planet carrier or ring, is held still.
Many modern automatic gearboxes have 8 to 10 forward gears.
At cruising speed many torque converters lock up, joining engine and gearbox directly to save fuel.
